bridges.mechanism: Escalations on the battlefield create urgent operational requirements and real-world testing opportunities that push armed forces and contractors to hurriedly field and scale AI-enabled sensors, targeting, and logistics systems.

Escalated kinetic activity (strikes, artillery, mines, logistics disruption) damages refinery infrastructure, forces evacuations or interrupts feedstock and transport, causing immediate drops in local refinery throughput and utilization.

Spikes in kinetic activity disrupt commodity flows, shipping routes and insurance costs, prompting firms and governments to diversify suppliers, stockpile critical inputs and reconfigure logistics, thereby increasing cross‑border supply‑chain resilience over the medium term.

Broad sanctions and export controls on dual-use technologies create precedents and political pressure that prompt governments and blocs to expand AI-related export controls, reporting rules, and oversight, raising overall regulatory attention.

New or tightened sanctions (banking, insurance, port access and shipping restrictions) directly block and delay shipments and financial settlement for diesel exports from affected suppliers, immediately reducing cross-border diesel flows.

Heightened sanctions regimes around the Russia–Ukraine war prompt governments to broaden and harden export‑control licensing and enforcement to prevent sanctioned diversion and close loopholes, leading to tighter controls that are then extended to technologies affecting US–China flows.

Rising defense-oriented funding and grants earmarked for the conflict expands budgets for robustness, red-teaming, and verification of AI systems as militaries and contractors allocate resources to ensure battlefield reliability and avoid catastrophic failures.

Surges in Western defense aid to Ukraine drive redeployment and longer forward-stationing of US/NATO naval and air assets to Europe, reducing patrols and real-time deterrence in the Red Sea/Gulf and thereby enabling more Houthi interdiction of shipping.

Sustained increases in Western defense aid to Ukraine signal a stronger US willingness to provide military backing to partners, which reduces Beijing's trust in US restraint and intentions toward regional contingencies.

Increased transfers of weapons and autonomous systems (drones, guided munitions) into the theatre multiplies the number of deployed AI-enabled platforms that can be captured, spoofed, exploited, or malfunction, raising the frequency of security incidents.

Larger and more visible arms deliveries to one side prompt retaliatory rhetoric, countermeasures and security posturing by opposing states, directly raising international political and security tensions that affect energy risk perceptions.

Increased volumes of arms transfers tied to the Russia‑Ukraine conflict (commercial or state-level diversions and barter deals) raise the flow of drones, cruise‑missile components and munitions into the region, enabling Iran‑aligned groups like the Houthis to mount more frequent and higher‑payload kinetic strikes.

Greater policy coordination among external allies increases market expectations of sustained coordinated restrictions or supply re-routing (and a higher risk premium), which raises diesel price levels even before additional physical supply changes occur.

Stronger cohesion among Western and regional partners preserves coordinated naval patrols, intelligence-sharing and combined strikes, which suppress Houthi attacks and reduce disruptions to maritime trade.

Greater cohesion among the US and its allies enables coordinated economic measures (harmonized tariffs, investment screening, and import bans) targeted at strategic competitors, raising aggregate trade restrictions between the US and China.

Increased high‑level and sustained bilateral diplomatic engagement reduces the likelihood of escalatory political moves and public confrontation, directly lowering international political tensions that threaten energy routes and contracts.

Higher‑level, sustained US–China diplomatic engagement sustains operational deconfliction and joint pressure channels (e.g., information sharing, coordinated naval escorts and diplomatic pressure on Tehran), which reduces successful Houthi attacks and thus maritime disruption.

Rising mutual strategic trust reduces perceived supply‑risk and risk premia in wholesale markets, prompting traders and buyers to scale back precautionary bids and insurance costs, putting downward pressure on diesel spot prices.

Rising bilateral strategic trust increases willingness by Washington and Beijing to intervene diplomatically and to restrain or publicly censure proxies, lowering the likelihood that localized incidents involving Iran/Houthis will spiral into broader reciprocal escalation.

Higher bilateral trade barriers shrink foreign market access and supply options, creating stronger domestic market and investor incentives to accelerate commercialization and scale local AI products to substitute for blocked imports.

An increase in bilateral trade restrictions (tariffs, quotas, export bans or sanctions) directly limits permissible shipments and adds clearance/insurance frictions, immediately reducing volumes of diesel and related distillates moved across borders.

Escalating US trade restrictions on China generate economic backlash among U.S. partners with large China exposure, creating policy rifts and bargaining frictions that weaken coordination and unity within the coalition responding to Russia.

Tighter export controls immediately restrict access to advanced GPUs, NPU accelerators and associated tooling for targeted firms, directly reducing their ability to train and operate large AI models at scale.

Tighter export controls on specialty catalysts, control systems and spare parts used in refining constrain access to critical inputs and maintenance supplies, causing unplanned outages and reduced run‑rates at affected refineries over time.

Tighter export controls (notably on dual‑use components) prompt alternative, covert transfers by actors seeking to evade sanctions—accelerating deliveries of drone/missile components to Iran and its Houthi proxies and enabling more frequent/higher‑capability strikes.

Tighter export controls on dual‑use technologies and upstream components reduce the availability of chips, guidance components and other inputs that China (and intermediaries) could re‑export or supply to Russian weapons producers, directly lowering the volume and tempo of arms and munitions reaching the conflict theatre.

More resilient, diversified and vetted cross‑border supply chains reduce the introduction of compromised hardware/software and provide redundancy for secure updates, directly lowering the frequency of AI system breaches and exploitations.

Visible use or testing of guided drones/missiles and evidence of autonomous targeting or AI-assisted guidance in kinetic strikes prompts lawmakers and regulators to accelerate constraints, export controls, and oversight on AI capabilities tied to weaponization.

Direct kinetic strikes on terminals, pipelines, storage or nearby infrastructure and the resultant security risks and workforce evacuations force temporary refinery shutdowns or capacity reductions, lowering utilization rates.

Increased Houthi/IRGC kinetic attacks pull Western naval and air assets, aerial refueling, and munitions stocks toward Middle Eastern contingencies, reducing available sorties, forward basing and materiel that would otherwise be applied to operations supporting/augmenting Ukrainian military intensity.

Spikes in missile/drone strikes on commercial or naval vessels prompt urgent US–China consultations and crisis‑management talks (deconfliction, rules of the road, information‑sharing) to prevent unintended escalation.

Acute interruptions to shipping and supply chains raise short‑term costs and investor pressure for rapid revenue growth, incentivizing startups and firms to accelerate AI product launches and monetization to shore up returns.

Attacks, seizures, inspections and mine risks in regional sea lanes and at ports force vessel reroutes, cancellations and port closures, directly reducing the volume of diesel/distillate shipments between regions.

Sustained Red Sea/Gulf of Aden interdiction forces rerouting, container and RO/RO shipment delays, and spikes in insurance/logistics costs that concretely delay or reduce sea-borne deliveries of weapons and heavy equipment destined for Ukraine.

Houthi interdictions and attacks on commercial shipping in the Red Sea and Gulf of Aden force large-scale rerouting, port congestion and longer transit times, directly degrading the robustness and adaptive capacity of cross‑border supply chains for autos, semiconductors and other sectors.
Physical interruptions to crude and refined product flows remove available supply from markets, tightening immediate balances and pushing spot and regional diesel prices higher.

Sustained crude/refined product shortages and price volatility create political pressure and energy‑security concerns that drive policymakers to tighten bilateral trade controls and sanctions screening (e.g., more stringent vetting, quotas or targeted embargoes) to limit exposure and transshipment risks.

A higher systemic likelihood of reciprocal escalation leads states and proxies to undertake more offensive cyber and influence operations, increasing attempts to breach, tamper with, or exfiltrate AI models and data.

A higher systemic likelihood that incidents will broaden increases diplomatic friction, sanctions risk and public risk premia, directly raising measured geopolitical tension levels among states and markets.

A higher likelihood that Middle Eastern incidents will broaden forces allied states to prioritize divergent regional responses (naval escorts, diplomatic outreach, bilateral deals), producing timing and policy disagreements that erode unity and coordinated policy toward the Russia‑Ukraine conflict.

A higher systemic likelihood that localized incidents will cascade increases mutual suspicion about the other's willingness to restrain proxies or to signal intentions, eroding perceived reliability and lowering bilateral strategic trust.

Commercial pressure drives firms to rapidly productize and export low‑cost autonomy and guidance stacks (flight-control, vision, navigation) that are repurposed by Houthis and other proxies into larger, more frequent anti-ship/drone swarm attacks, increasing maritime disruption.

Intense market and investor pressure to commercialize and export AI products increases cross‑border transfers and high‑visibility sales, provoking regulators to tighten export controls to limit perceived technology leakage and national security exposure.

Wider deployment of AI-driven freight-matching, routing and real-time logistics platforms increases cargo turnover and reduces frictions, producing a measurable rise in short-term cross-border shipments of diesel and related distillates.

Wide-scale rollouts of commercially available AI perception and autonomy models make high-performance guidance and target-recognition components readily available for integration into loitering munitions and guided drones, raising the frequency and lethality of kinetic strikes by proxies.

Wider operational deployment of AI-enabled ISR, targeting aids and autonomous munitions increases strike tempo and target discrimination capacity on the battlefield, enabling higher-frequency and more precise kinetic operations.

Rapid, large‑scale rollouts of compute‑intensive AI services spike demand for semiconductors, optical components and specialized hardware, creating bottlenecks and single‑supplier dependencies that reduce cross‑border supply‑chain resilience.

Regulatory actions imposing audits, temporary certifications, or restrictions on AI/automated control systems used in refining prompt precautionary outages or deratings while firms implement compliance fixes, lowering utilization rates.

Stronger regulatory attention and stricter export controls on dual‑use AI systems reduce legal transfer channels and commercial availability of autonomy/targeting software to non-state actors, lowering their ability to conduct precision kinetic attacks.

New or tightened AI export controls, reporting requirements and entity-designation authorities provide legal and procedural tools that governments can rapidly apply to restrict AI-related services and companies tied to Russia, expanding and intensifying sanctions and restrictions.

High-frequency security incidents involving AI (e.g., cross-border adversarial attacks on critical systems or high-profile attribution of state-linked exploits) provoke diplomatic disputes, retaliatory measures, and sanctions that raise interstate political and security tensions affecting energy routes and markets.

Cybersecurity incidents that compromise AI-driven operational technology or trigger integrity concerns force refineries to throttle, halt, or run on manual/interim controls for safety, directly reducing refinery utilization.

A rise in AI-related breaches or attribution‑contentious intrusions affecting allied systems generates mutual suspicion over supply chains and sharing, degrading trust and coordination among partners responding to the conflict.

High-frequency AI security incidents that are attributed to or leak into the other side (e.g., model theft, data exfiltration, AI-enabled cyberattacks) produce immediate reciprocal suspicion and public pressure, reducing bilateral strategic trust.

Visible breaches or exploits demonstrating dual‑use AI capabilities prompt policymakers to tighten export controls and licensing (e.g., restricting model weights, tooling, or chip exports) to prevent further cross‑border spillovers.

Increased funding for red-teaming, verification and safety controls reduces the incidence of false positives, runaway automation or unintended targeting behaviors that could trigger accidental escalatory strikes, lowering overall kinetic intensity.

Increased domestic refinery utilization lowers dependence on external (including Russian) fuel supplies, strengthening policymakers' ability and willingness to maintain or escalate economic restrictions, thereby increasing sanctions pressure.

Higher diesel stocks in theatre and supply lines enable sustained mechanized and logistics operations (vehicle movement, artillery resupply, air sortie support), directly increasing the tempo and scale of kinetic operations.

Higher volumes of diesel and distillates transiting chokepoints (e.g., Bab al‑Mandeb/Red Sea) increase the number of vulnerable commercial targets and transit interactions, raising incentives and opportunities for Houthi interdiction and thereby increasing maritime disruption.

Higher volumes and reliability of cross-border shipments reduce transit bottlenecks and delays for physical delivery of weapons and munitions into and around the conflict zone, increasing the rate and volume of transfers.

Sustained drops in diesel and distillate shipments raise transport disruptions and variability in delivery times, directly degrading the robustness and recoverability of cross-border manufacturing supply chains for autos, semiconductors and batteries.

A sharp rise in diesel prices increases electricity and logistics operating costs for cloud providers and edge operators (via higher grid generation and backup fuel costs), eroding margins and investor appetite for rapid, capital‑intensive AI rollouts and thus lowering market pressure to commercialize new models quickly.

Rising diesel prices make seizing fuel, extorting shippers, or attacking fuel infrastructure materially more lucrative, incentivizing additional Houthi kinetic operations against tankers, terminals, and supply routes.

A persistent surge in diesel costs raises domestic production and logistics pressures, prompting policymakers to adopt protective tariffs, quotas or subsidies to shield sensitive industries and thus increase trade restrictions between the sides.

Rising geopolitical tensions raise incentives for state and proxy actors to conduct cyber‑operations and supply‑chain attacks targeting AI infrastructure for espionage, disruption or coercion, directly increasing the frequency of security incidents against AI systems and platforms.

Elevated geopolitical tension increases the frequency of naval escorts, interdictions, punitive strikes, and retaliatory actions in the theater, which directly raises the probability and scale of physical disruptions to crude and refined oil shipments.

Rising energy-related diplomatic frictions and security incidents among partners (e.g., disputes over transit, diversion of supplies) produce unilateral national measures and political friction that erode coordination and policy alignment within allied coalitions.

Acute increases in energy-route or supplier-targeted political friction (e.g., sanctions, seizures, naval incidents) directly reduce bilateral confidence by signaling hostile intent and prompting mutual threat reassessments.

Rising energy-related geopolitical tensions prompt authorities to tighten export licensing and broaden controls on equipment and technologies deemed useful to an adversary, increasing overall export-control stringency toward the other side.

Military engagement intensity
nodes.description: Measures the overall tempo, scale and kinetic intensity of armed operations (air strikes, drone attacks, artillery, maneuvers) across the conflict environment.

nodes.label: Air defense effectiveness
nodes.description: Measures the capacity and success rate of air-defense systems and countermeasures to detect and neutralize aerial threats.

nodes.label: Infrastructure damage level
nodes.description: Measures the cumulative physical destruction to critical economic, transport and energy infrastructure caused by hostilities.

nodes.label: Energy supply disruption rate
nodes.description: Measures the rate and magnitude of interruptions to energy production, transit and deliveries affecting markets and consumers.

nodes.label: Sanctions and restrictions pressure
nodes.description: Measures the breadth, intensity and enforcement of external economic and financial restrictive measures applied to actors linked to the conflict.

nodes.label: Asset control and seizure extent
nodes.description: Measures the share and value of foreign or contested assets that are frozen, seized, placed under control, or otherwise restricted.

nodes.label: Defense financial support flow
nodes.description: Measures the rate of incoming financial assistance and budgetary transfers earmarked for defence, security and reconstruction related to the conflict.

nodes.label: Arms transfer volume
nodes.description: Measures the volume and frequency of transfers of weapons, munitions and military equipment into and around the conflict theatre.

nodes.label: Cyber attack activity
nodes.description: Measures the frequency, sophistication and impact of offensive cyber operations targeting infrastructure, communications and political systems.

nodes.label: Information polarization level
nodes.description: Measures the degree of societal and media polarization, misinformation intensity, and competing narratives about the conflict.

nodes.label: Electoral legitimacy perception
nodes.description: Measures public and external confidence in the fairness, representativeness and legitimacy of political processes occurring during the conflict.

nodes.label: Displaced population stock
nodes.description: Measures the cumulative number of civilians displaced internally or across borders as a result of hostilities and insecurity.

nodes.label: Humanitarian needs severity
nodes.description: Measures the scale and severity of acute humanitarian needs including casualties, medical care requirements, food insecurity and shelter shortages.

nodes.label: Economic interdependence strain
nodes.description: Measures the degree to which cross-border trade, investment, financial ties and energy interdependencies are disrupted, politicized or rerouted.

nodes.label: Transnational crime flow
nodes.description: Measures the rate and scale of cross-border criminal activity and illicit economic flows (fraud, smuggling, exploitation) amplified by the conflict environment.

nodes.label: Alliance cohesion
nodes.description: Measures the degree of coordination, unity of purpose and policy alignment among external security and political partners responding to the conflict.

nodes.label: Economic interdependence

nodes.label: Trade restriction level
nodes.description: The aggregate intensity of tariffs, quotas and non‑tariff measures constraining bilateral trade.

nodes.label: Technology governance dialogue intensity

nodes.label: Export control stringency

nodes.label: Critical minerals supply concentration
nodes.description: The geographic and supplier concentration of critical minerals and rare earth supply chains.

nodes.label: Supply chain resilience
nodes.description: The robustness and adaptive capacity of cross‑border supply chains for key sectors (autos, semiconductors, batteries).

nodes.label: Military posture level
nodes.description: The scale and readiness of military presence, deployments and power‑projection activities in contested regions.

nodes.label: Alliance and partner cohesion
nodes.description: The degree of policy alignment and coordinated action among third‑party allies and partners relevant to the bilateral relationship.

nodes.label: Corporate financial stress
nodes.description: The level of financial strain across corporate sectors exposed to the bilateral relationship, including profits, writedowns and restructuring pressure.

nodes.label: Financial market volatility
nodes.description: The amplitude and frequency of price swings in equity, bond and currency markets tied to geopolitical and summit developments.

nodes.label: Cross‑border regulatory intervention rate
nodes.description: The rate at which new regulatory actions, investigations or enforcement measures affecting cross‑border commerce are initiated.

nodes.label: Skilled labor mobility
nodes.description: The ease and volume of cross‑border movement of skilled workers, executives and technical personnel.

nodes.label: Public confidence in summit outcomes
nodes.description: The level of public and political confidence that summit negotiations will produce stable, predictable outcomes.

nodes.label: Cyber and AI security incident frequency
nodes.description: The rate of cyberattacks, AI‑related security incidents and public disclosures that affect bilateral technology and security dynamics.

nodes.description: The aggregate frequency and destructive power of cross-border missile, drone, and direct-kinetic strikes in the theater.

nodes.label: Proxy force capability
nodes.description: The combat strength, logistical sustainment, and operational reach of irregular or proxy armed groups active in the region.

nodes.label: External military posturing
nodes.description: The scale and tempo of visible force deployments, patrols, and show-of-force operations by external armed actors around the conflict zone.

nodes.label: Diplomatic engagement rate
nodes.description: The rate and intensity of formal and informal diplomatic contacts, negotiations, and public signaling among relevant actors.

nodes.label: Air defense capability
nodes.description: The readiness, coverage, and effectiveness of integrated air-defense systems protecting population centers and critical infrastructure.

nodes.label: Maritime trade disruption level
nodes.description: The current degree to which shipping routes, ports, and maritime commerce are interrupted by insecurity or interdiction.

nodes.label: Energy market volatility
nodes.description: The magnitude of short-term price swings and trading volatility in energy commodities driven by security and supply uncertainty.

nodes.label: Oil supply disruption
nodes.description: The rate at which physical crude oil and refined product availability is reduced or rerouted due to security incidents or blockades.

nodes.label: Financial market risk premium
nodes.description: The elevation of risk pricing in equity, bond, and currency markets reflecting perceived geopolitical risk in the region.

nodes.label: Travel and security advisory level
nodes.description: The prevailing intensity of public warnings, travel restrictions, and private-sector risk assessments affecting movement to and within the region.

nodes.label: Domestic political pressure
nodes.description: The strength of internal political demands, protest activity, and public opinion pushing leaders toward restraint or retaliation.

nodes.label: Alliance cohesion strength
nodes.description: The degree of strategic alignment, burden-sharing, and unified policy among partner actors coordinating responses to the crisis.

nodes.label: Arms procurement rate
nodes.description: The speed and volume at which actors acquire, transfer, or deploy weapons, munitions, and enabling military systems.

nodes.label: Human displacement rate
nodes.description: The flow of civilians relocating or fleeing conflict-affected areas per unit time due to insecurity and damage to livelihoods.

nodes.label: Intelligence sharing level
nodes.description: The depth, timeliness, and operational integration of actionable information exchanged among security actors.

nodes.label: Escalation propensity
nodes.description: The systemic likelihood that localized incidents will trigger reciprocal responses and broaden into higher‑intensity or wider conflict.

Model capability
nodes.description: The aggregate technical capability and performance level of advanced AI models (ability to perform tasks, generalize, and operate autonomously).

nodes.label: Commercialization pressure
nodes.description: The intensity of market and investor-driven incentives to release, scale, and monetize AI systems rapidly.

nodes.label: Capital availability
nodes.description: The quantity of investment and financing accessible to organizations developing and deploying advanced AI systems.

nodes.label: Cash burn rate
nodes.description: The rate at which organizations expend financial resources to train, operate, and scale AI systems.

nodes.label: Deployment scale
nodes.description: The extent and frequency of AI model rollouts and active production deployments across applications and users.

nodes.label: Safety evaluation capacity
nodes.description: The available technical, methodological, and organizational capability to conduct independent safety testing and audits of AI systems.

nodes.label: Regulatory pressure
nodes.description: The level of policy, legislative, and enforcement attention imposing constraints, reporting, or requirements on AI development and deployment.

nodes.label: Security incident rate
nodes.description: The frequency at which AI systems experience breaches, exploitations, unauthorized access, or breakout behaviors.

nodes.label: Adversarial activity
nodes.description: The intensity and sophistication of malicious actors exploiting or weaponizing AI systems and related infrastructure.

nodes.label: Model malfunction rate
nodes.description: The rate at which deployed models produce incorrect, harmful, or operationally failing outputs in real-world use.

nodes.label: Public trust
nodes.description: The average level of public confidence in AI technologies and the organizations that provide them.

nodes.label: Media attention
nodes.description: The intensity and salience of news and public discourse focused on AI developments, incidents, and debates.

nodes.label: Compute capacity
nodes.description: The available computing infrastructure (training and inference throughput) that enables large-scale model development and operation.

nodes.label: Data availability
nodes.description: The volume, diversity, and accessibility of data resources usable for training and fine-tuning AI models.

nodes.label: Legal liability risk
nodes.description: The perceived and actual exposure to lawsuits, regulatory penalties, and legal costs stemming from AI harms or breaches.

nodes.label: Safety investment rate
nodes.description: The flow of funding and resources directed specifically toward AI safety research, red-teaming, and oversight mechanisms.

Middle-distillate production flow
nodes.description: The volumetric rate at which refineries produce diesel and other middle-distillate fuels for the market.

nodes.label: Refinery conversion capacity
nodes.description: The aggregated maximum capability of refining infrastructure to convert crude oil into middle-distillate products.

nodes.label: Refinery utilization rate
nodes.description: The proportion of available refining capacity that is actively operating at a given time.

nodes.label: Diesel storage inventory
nodes.description: The total volume of diesel and equivalent middle-distillate held in commercial and strategic storage across the system.

nodes.label: Tanker availability and capacity
nodes.description: The effective shipping tonnage and number of tankers available for transporting middle distillates across shipping routes.

nodes.label: Freight rate level
nodes.description: The prevailing cost per unit-distance to move middle-distillate cargoes by sea, reflecting shipping market tightness.

nodes.label: Cross-border trade flow volumes
nodes.description: The volume of diesel and related distillates shipped between regions and countries per unit time.

nodes.label: Domestic consumption rate
nodes.description: The rate at which end-users within consuming regions are burning or using diesel for transport, industry, and agriculture.

nodes.label: Alternative fuel substitution rate
nodes.description: The rate at which diesel demand is replaced by alternatives (e.g., biodiesel blends, LNG, electrification) over time.

nodes.label: Diesel price level
nodes.description: The market price per unit of diesel, reflecting current supply-demand balance and market signals.

nodes.label: Price volatility
nodes.description: The short- to medium-term variability and amplitude of fluctuations in diesel and middle-distillate prices.

nodes.label: Export restrictions intensity
nodes.description: The degree to which policy frameworks constrain or limit cross-border exports of diesel and middle distillates.

nodes.label: Fuel subsidy and rationing intensity
nodes.description: The scale and prevalence of domestic interventions such as subsidies, price controls, and rationing applied to diesel consumers.

nodes.label: Shipping network congestion
nodes.description: The level of logistical bottlenecks and capacity constraints in maritime and port networks relevant to distillate movements.

nodes.label: Storage drawdown rate
nodes.description: The pace at which diesel inventories are being depleted from storage reservoirs over a given period.

nodes.label: Geopolitical tension level
nodes.description: The intensity of international political and security frictions that affect energy supply routes, trade relationships, and market risk perceptions.
